content: Certainly. For patients weighing more than 60 kg, the recommended dosage is 400 mg taken orally twice daily for a duration of 8 to 30 days. For patients weighing less than 60 kg, the dosage is calculated as 15 mg/kg/day, divided into two doses taken orally, with a maximum daily dose not exceeding 800 mg. This regimen is also followed for 8 to 30 days. For patients weighing more than 60 kg undergoing a cyclic treatment, the dosage is 400 mg taken orally twice daily for 28 days, followed by a 14-day drug-free period. This cycle is repeated three times. For patients weighing less than 60 kg, the dosage remains 15 mg/kg/day, divided into two doses, with a maximum daily dose of 800 mg. This is administered for 28 days, followed by a 14-day drug-free period, repeated for three cycles. Additional dosing regimens include: 400 mg taken orally once daily for 10 days. 400 mg taken orally once daily for 3 days. 400 mg taken orally twice daily for 5 days. A single 400 mg dose taken orally, with a repeat dose after 2 weeks. 10 mg/kg taken orally once daily for 7 days. 400 mg taken orally twice daily for 21 days. Administration Instructions: Always take this medication with food to enhance absorption. Regular monitoring of complete blood count (CBC) and liver function tests (LFTs) is essential during treatment. Drug Interactions: 1. Ropinterferon alfa-2b and Albendazole: These drugs can increase each other's toxicity. Avoid co-administration or use alternative therapies. Both agents are myelosuppressive and may lead to additive bone marrow suppression. If used together, monitor for excessive myelosuppression. 2. Acalabrutinib and Albendazole: Co-administration may increase the risk of myelosuppressive effects due to pharmacodynamic synergy. Use with caution and monitor closely. 3. Fosphenytoin and Albendazole: Fosphenytoin increases the metabolism of albendazole, reducing its active metabolite levels. Monitor for decreased efficacy and use with caution. 4. Grapefruit: Grapefruit increases albendazole levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid grapefruit or monitor closely if consumed. 5. Phenytoin and Albendazole: Phenytoin reduces albendazole levels by increasing its metabolism. Monitor for reduced efficacy. 6. Dexamethasone and Albendazole: Dexamethasone increases albendazole levels through an unspecified mechanism. The clinical significance is unclear, but monitoring is advised. 7. Praziquantel and Albendazole: Praziquantel increases albendazole levels through an unspecified mechanism. The clinical significance is unclear, but monitoring is advised. Warnings and Precautions: Bone Marrow Suppression: Albendazole may cause bone marrow suppression, aplastic anemia, and agranulocytosis. Monitor blood counts at the start of each 28-day cycle and every 2 weeks during therapy. Discontinue treatment if significant changes in blood counts occur. Neurocysticercosis: Treatment with albendazole may unmask pre-existing neurocysticercosis, presenting with neurological symptoms such as seizures or increased intracranial pressure. Treat promptly with corticosteroids and anticonvulsants. Pregnancy: Albendazole may harm a developing fetus. Women of reproductive potential should undergo pregnancy testing before starting therapy and use effective contraception during treatment and for 3 days after the last dose. Discontinue therapy if pregnancy occurs and inform the patient of potential risks to the fetus. Retinal Damage: Retinal involvement has been reported in cases of retinal cysticercosis. Examine patients for retinal lesions before initiating therapy for neurocysticercosis. Hepatotoxicity: Reversible elevations in liver enzymes may occur. Monitor liver enzymes before starting each treatment cycle and every 2 weeks during therapy. Discontinue treatment if liver enzyme levels exceed twice the upper limit of normal. Patients with hepatic echinococcosis or abnormal LFTs are at increased risk of hepatotoxicity. Breastfeeding: Albendazole and its active metabolite, albendazole sulfoxide, are present in low concentrations in breast milk. No adverse effects on breastfed infants have been reported. Consider the benefits of breastfeeding alongside the mother’s clinical need for the medication. Pharmacokinetics: Absorption: Less than 5% is absorbed; absorption increases 4-5 times with a fatty meal. Distribution: Penetrates well into hydatid cysts and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Protein binding is approximately 70%. Metabolism: Extensively metabolized in the liver via first-pass metabolism, primarily through sulfoxidation. Half-life: 8-12 hours. Excretion: Less than 1% is excreted in urine as active metabolites; the majority is excreted in feces. Side Effects: Common side effects include nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, headache, and temporary hair loss. Serious allergic reactions are rare. Contact a healthcare provider if severe side effects occur. Storage: Store at room temperature, away from light and moisture. Do not store in the bathroom. Properly discard expired or unused medication. Missed Dose: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered. If it is near the time of the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume the regular schedule. Do not double the dose. Overdose: In case of overdose, seek immediate medical attention. In the U.S., contact poison control at 1-800-222-1222. Important Notes: This information is a summary and does not include all possible details about the medication. Always consult a healthcare professional for complete guidance tailored to individual health needs.
